thread.title: Here’s what repatriation means for the dollar and Treasurys - MarketWatch

author: Anneken Tappe
title: Here’s what repatriation means for the dollar and Treasurys - MarketWatch
text:
Published: Jan 18, 2018 3:54 p.m. ET Share 
By Anneken Tappe 
As a sweeping tax overhaul becomes reality, investors are wondering whether the repatriation of foreign profits will provide a lift to the ailing U.S. dollar or weigh on Treasurys. 
On Wednesday, tech giant Apple Inc. AAPL, +0.08% said it would make a one-time $38 billion tax payment related to offshore cash holdings under the new law—a move that prompted speculation other companies could soon act to repatriate their overseas cash holdings. 
Also see: Tax bill lowered corporate tax rate, so why are some companies announcing charges? 
Still, analysts remain skeptical of the effect this move by Apple and its peers could have on foreign exchange and Treasury markets. 
“There is about $2.5 to $3 trillion abroad,” said Derek Halpenny, European head of global markets research at MUFG, “and around 80% of that is already U.S. dollar-denominated.” 
Apple and its peers Microsoft Inc. MSFT, -0.06% Google parent Alphabet Inc. GOOG, -0.23% Facebook Inc. FB, +1.44% and Amazon.com Inc. AMZN, -0.12% hold just shy of $250 billion of government paper, according to their corporate filings in the second quarter of 2017, according to Deutsche Bank. 
Some estimates put the proportion of dollar-denominated assets as high as 95%, according to Mark McCormick, North America head of FX Strategy at TD Securities, noting that the foreign exchange market only cares about the money denominated in other currencies that would have to be converted. 
Opinion: Apple’s tax shift means less cash than you think—but still plenty for a big acquisition 
To put it in context, global foreign exchange is a $3 trillion spot market, and the U.S. current-account deficit is $550 billion, McCormick said. So Apple’s repatriation, even though it is one of the largest holders of foreign assets, will likely not really move the needle. 
Further, Halpenny said “it’s hard to garner how much of what they released was already going to happen anyway.” Maybe the next corporate earnings cycle will bring more clarity, he said, adding that it might also provide more guidance regarding share buybacks, which are expected to be a popular way for companies to use their overseas cash. 
Corporations will also have an eight-year window to take action on their repatriation of assets, which “reduces the risks of a ‘chunky’ flow of capital moving through the market at once,” McCormick said. 
“There won’t be significant impact on FX,” said Halpenny. “Overnight, Treasurys moved up a little on the promise that there could be additional liquidity when money is being moved. But a lot of holdings are in corporate bonds rather than in Treasurys,” he added. 
The yield on the U.S. 10-year note TMUBMUSD10Y, +1.29% touched its highest level since March 2017 on Thursday. They last yielded 2.61%, according to FactSet. 
Repatriation “is only a small risk to the story of the flattening yield curve,” agreed John Herrmann, MUFG’s U.S. rates strategist. The U.S. government bond yield curve has flattened significantly over the past year, despite hawkish monetary policy from the Federal Reserve. 
“While some blamed the selloff on Apple’s 10K filing—large tax bill and investment in the U.S.—the failure of corporate [bond] spreads to follow through suggests this wasn’t the actual catalyst for the move,” said Aaron Kohli, fixed-income strategist for BMO Capital Markets, in a note. 
Who could benefit, on the other hand, are equity holders, because companies are expected to use their repatriated money for share buybacks and to pay dividends, neither of which is the kind of economically stimulating investment activity politicians likely had in mind when devising the plan. 
“Indeed, another equity boost could offer tailwinds to global financial conditions, reinforcing the reflation trade and policy normalization outside the U.S. For the dollar DXY, -0.44% this backdrop would further hinder it—not rescue it,” McCormick said.
